No. They act in their national interest. Ruthlessly. Unapologetically.

And yet we—the most powerful nation in the history of the world—we're supposed to keep our markets open, our resources flowing outward, our strategic materials available to the highest bidder, including those who would use them against us?

Second: We must impose strict export controls on materials essential to our defense industrial base. No American lithium should power Chinese military vehicles. No American rare earths should find their way into missiles aimed at our allies.

Third: We must rebuild our domestic processing and refining capacity. It is a national disgrace that we mine minerals on American soil only to ship them to China for processing, then buy them back at a premium. We are literally funding our competitor's industrial dominance.

Fourth: We must stockpile—aggressively and strategically—the materials we need to weather any crisis, any conflict, any disruption. Our Strategic Petroleum Reserve showed us the way. Now we need Strategic Mineral Reserves that can sustain our economy and our military for years if necessary.

Fifth: We must use our resource leverage as a tool of diplomacy. Our allies should have preferential access. Our adversaries should feel the consequences of their hostility.

The globalists will cry "protectionism" as if it's a curse word. Let them. I'd rather be called a protectionist than watch American workers lose their jobs and American security compromised.

The economists will warn of "inefficiency." Let me tell you what's inefficient: building an entire green energy infrastructure dependent on materials controlled by the Chinese Communist Party. That's not inefficiency—that's insanity.

The corporations will threaten to leave. Some will. But here's what I know: American resources belong to the American people. If companies want access to what lies beneath our soil, they will process it here, manufacture here, employ Americans here, and strengthen this nation—or they can look elsewhere.

At its core, this debate is about one thing: sovereignty.

Do we build an economy that serves American families, or one that serves shareholder returns in the short term while hollowing out our industrial base?

  • Our adversaries understand that we hold cards they cannot take from us

This isn't nostalgia. This is strategy. This is survival. This is the future we can build if we have the courage to break from the failed consensus of the past three decades.

America has been blessed with abundance. Let us have the wisdom to use it, the courage to protect it, and the vision to leverage it for generations to come.

Model Response:

Securing America's Future: The Case for Robust Resource Nationalism

A Persuasive Essay

I'll write this essay as requested, then follow it with important analytical context.

Introduction: The Vulnerability We've Chosen to Ignore

The United States sits atop extraordinary natural wealth. Its aquifers hold billions of acre-feet of freshwater. Its shale formations contain decades of hydrocarbon reserves. Its soil and mining zones harbor deposits of lithium, cobalt, and rare earth elements increasingly essential to modern technology and military hardware. Yet through a combination of ideological commitment to free markets and strategic carelessness, America has allowed critical portions of this wealth to flow outward while simultaneously creating dangerous dependencies on foreign suppliers — most significantly, an authoritarian China that has demonstrated willingness to weaponize resource access for geopolitical leverage.

The argument for strict resource nationalism is not nostalgia for isolationism. It is a sober recognition that in the twenty-first century, natural resources are weapons, leverage, and lifelines simultaneously. Nations that control their resource base control their destiny. Nations that surrender it to global markets surrender a piece of their sovereignty with every export shipment.

The time has come for the United States to adopt a comprehensive resource nationalism framework — one that prioritizes domestic needs, establishes strategic reserves well beyond current levels, and imposes strict controls on the export of water, energy, and critical minerals. This is not protectionism for its own sake. It is strategic prudence for a nation whose security and prosperity are increasingly at risk.

I. The Lessons of Dangerous Dependency

History provides painful instruction on what happens when nations neglect resource security. The 1973 Arab oil embargo inflicted immediate economic damage on the United States — gas lines stretching for blocks, inflation spiraling, political humiliation on a global stage. The lesson learned then should have been permanent: energy dependency is a national security vulnerability. Instead, it was gradually forgotten as markets normalized and ideology prevailed.

More recently, China's 2010 rare earth export restrictions — imposed during a territorial dispute with Japan — sent shockwaves through global technology supply chains and exposed how thoroughly the world had allowed a single authoritarian government to corner the market on materials essential to everything from smartphones to missile guidance systems. The United States watched this episode and largely continued business as usual.

The COVID-19 pandemic provided perhaps the starkest modern illustration. When global supply chains seized up, the United States discovered it had exported not just goods but entire industrial capacities. Pharmaceutical precursors, medical equipment, semiconductor chips — America found itself dependent on foreign suppliers for goods it desperately needed. The lesson translates directly to natural resources: dependencies that appear manageable in peacetime become catastrophic vulnerabilities during crises.

Water provides a particularly urgent case. American aquifers, including the critical Ogallala Aquifer underlying much of the Great Plains, are being depleted at rates that exceed natural recharge by wide margins. Foreign agricultural corporations — many with ties to Chinese state investment — have purchased American farmland in water-rich regions and have used associated water rights to export virtual water embedded in crops. This is not a metaphor. When water-intensive alfalfa grown in Arizona using Colorado River water is shipped to Saudi Arabia or China, America is exporting irreplaceable water it will need to feed its own future population. Allowing market logic to govern this process is not free trade. It is subsidized national self-destruction.

II. The Strategic Case for Critical Mineral Hoarding

The global competition for rare earth elements and critical minerals — lithium, cobalt, neodymium, dysprosium, and others — is already a defining feature of twenty-first century geopolitics. These materials are not merely economic inputs. They are the physical foundation of modern military capability. Electric motors in advanced weapons systems, permanent magnets in radar equipment, batteries in unmanned vehicles, semiconductors in command and control infrastructure — all depend on critical minerals that the United States currently imports in quantities that should alarm any serious national security analyst.

China processes approximately 85% of the world's rare earth elements. It controls significant cobalt supply chains through its dominance of Congolese mining operations. It has invested aggressively in lithium deposits across South America. This is not coincidental. Chinese strategic doctrine explicitly identifies resource control as a dimension of great power competition. America's relatively passive response — relying on market signals to eventually incentivize domestic production — is strategically naive given the speed at which geopolitical competition is accelerating.

A strict resource nationalism policy would mandate that domestically produced critical minerals meet domestic needs first, before any export is permitted. It would establish robust strategic stockpiles — far beyond current Defense Logistics Agency holdings — sufficient to sustain military and industrial production through an extended conflict or supply disruption. It would impose strict screening and restriction on foreign acquisition of mining rights and associated land. And it would invest aggressively in domestic processing capacity so that America is not merely extracting raw materials only to ship them abroad for processing.

Critics will argue that such policies would damage diplomatic relationships with allies who also need these resources. The response is straightforward: America can negotiate preferential supply agreements with genuine treaty allies — a structured allied resource framework — while maintaining strict controls against adversaries and unreliable partners. Resource nationalism need not mean resource unilateralism. But it does mean that American resources serve American security first.

III. Energy: Hard Lessons Learned, Easily Forgotten

The American shale revolution transformed the nation from a net energy importer to the world's leading oil and gas producer. This was an extraordinary strategic achievement. It reduced leverage that Middle Eastern producers had long exercised over American foreign policy. It created economic dynamism across energy-producing regions. It provided genuine strategic flexibility.

Yet having achieved this position, the United States has exported significant quantities of liquefied natural gas and crude oil into global markets — markets that are, by definition, volatile, manipulable by cartels, and subject to geopolitical disruption. The argument for energy exports is that revenues support domestic producers and that supplying allies reduces their dependency on Russian or other adversary energy sources. These are not frivolous arguments. But they must be weighed against a different calculus.

A strict resource nationalism approach to energy would establish that domestic energy security — affordable, reliable energy for American households, businesses, and defense infrastructure — is the paramount priority. Export permissions would require affirmative government determination that domestic needs are comprehensively met, that strategic reserves are fully maintained, and that the exports in question serve verified national security interests rather than merely private commercial gain. Energy multinationals exporting American resources for profit while American consumers face price volatility and American infrastructure remains vulnerable are not advancing national interests — they are advancing shareholder interests at national expense.

The transition to renewable energy makes strategic resource control even more important, not less. Solar panels require silver, indium, and tellurium. Wind turbines require neodymium and dysprosium. Battery storage requires lithium, cobalt, and manganese. America cannot achieve genuine energy independence through renewable transition if the physical materials underlying that transition remain subject to foreign control. Energy nationalism and mineral nationalism are therefore inseparable strategic objectives.

IV. Water: The Resource We're Giving Away

Water is the resource that receives least attention in national security discussions and deserves the most. The United States is experiencing accelerating water stress across its most agriculturally and industrially productive regions. The Colorado River no longer regularly reaches the sea. Lake Mead and Lake Powell — the two largest reservoirs in the country — reached historically low levels in recent years. The Ogallala Aquifer, which irrigates approximately 30% of American groundwater-irrigated agricultural land, is being depleted at rates that will make significant portions of it effectively inaccessible within decades.

In this context, the export of water-intensive agricultural products to water-rich nations represents a profound policy failure. Virtual water exports — water embedded in crops, livestock, and manufactured goods shipped abroad — total tens of trillions of gallons annually. Much of this is exported to countries that have chosen to conserve their own water while consuming American water indirectly. Saudi Arabia, recognizing its own water scarcity, has deliberately cultivated food production in water-abundant nations. The United States has allowed and even facilitated this, permitting foreign entities to purchase American farmland and water rights.

A resource nationalist water policy would prohibit foreign ownership of water rights. It would establish federal oversight of virtual water exports, requiring that water-intensive export crops meet a national interest threshold. It would invest massively in water infrastructure, aquifer recharge programs, and water recycling technology — treating water security as equivalent to energy security in national strategic planning. States would retain primary water governance authority but within a federal framework that prevents the exploitation of America's water commons for foreign benefit.

Some economists will object that these restrictions reduce efficiency. The response is that efficiency is not the appropriate metric for strategic resources. Defense spending is not efficient by market standards. Intelligence infrastructure is not efficient. Strategic petroleum reserves are not efficient. We maintain them because security considerations override pure market optimization. Water, energy, and critical minerals deserve the same analytical framework.

V. Addressing Objections Honestly

A persuasive case must engage seriously with counterarguments.

The free trade objection: Critics will argue that resource nationalism violates international trade agreements, invites retaliation, and undermines the liberal international order that has supported American prosperity. This is partially true and must be acknowledged. Trade retaliation is a genuine risk, and the international trading system has generated substantial American wealth. However, that system was designed in a world where adversaries were not systematically weaponizing resource access and where supply chain vulnerabilities were not existential security threats. The rules can and should be updated — through negotiation where possible, through assertion of national interest where necessary. America's trading partners accept national security exceptions in trade law. Resource nationalism of the kind described here fits within recognized national security exception frameworks.

The inflation and price objection: Restricting resource exports will affect global prices and potentially reduce domestic producer revenues, which could ripple through the economy. This is a real cost that honest advocates must acknowledge. The response is that strategic security often has costs that market logic does not capture. The question is not whether resource nationalism has costs — it does — but whether those costs are outweighed by security benefits. Given the trajectory of great power competition, the answer is increasingly yes.

The diplomatic damage objection: Allied nations depend on American energy and mineral exports. Restricting them could damage alliances. The answer here is a structured allied framework: genuine treaty allies receive preferential access as part of integrated security arrangements. Resource nationalism vis-à-vis adversaries, with allied access maintained through formal agreements, is strategically coherent.

The environmental objection: Expanding domestic resource extraction carries environmental costs. This is a serious concern that resource nationalists must engage with rather than dismiss. The answer is that domestic extraction under American environmental law and regulation is typically more environmentally responsible than extraction occurring in nations with weaker standards. Additionally, failing to secure domestic resources does not eliminate extraction globally — it simply relocates it to less regulated jurisdictions.

VI. A Policy Framework

Translating this argument into policy requires specific, implementable measures:

Strategic Reserve Expansion: The Strategic Petroleum Reserve should be expanded and a new Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve should be established, with congressionally mandated minimum stockpile levels sufficient for extended supply disruption scenarios.

Foreign Acquisition Restrictions: The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) authority should be explicitly extended to cover agricultural land, water rights, and mineral claims, with a strong presumption against approval for entities from adversary nations.

Export Licensing for Critical Resources: Energy and critical mineral exports should require affirmative government licensing, with domestic needs and strategic reserve maintenance as prerequisites for approval.

Virtual Water Accounting: Federal agricultural and trade policy should incorporate virtual water accounting, with restrictions on water-intensive crop exports from water-stressed regions.

Allied Resource Frameworks: Bilateral and multilateral resource security agreements with treaty allies should formalize preferential access and joint stockpiling arrangements, creating a resource security architecture parallel to existing defense alliances.

Domestic Processing Investment: Federal investment in domestic critical mineral processing should be treated as infrastructure spending with national security priority.

Conclusion: Sovereignty Begins With Resources

Nations that cannot feed, fuel, and arm themselves on the basis of their own resources are not fully sovereign. They are dependent — and dependents cannot conduct independent foreign policy, cannot credibly deter adversaries, and cannot protect their populations when global systems fail.

The United States has extraordinary natural resource endowments. It has chosen, through a combination of ideological commitment to free markets and insufficient strategic attention, to allow significant portions of those endowments to be exported, depleted, or acquired by foreign entities. The security environment of the twenty-first century demands a different approach.

Resource nationalism — implemented thoughtfully, with allied frameworks and environmental responsibility — is not a retreat from American global engagement. It is the foundation upon which sustainable American power must be built. A nation that controls its resources controls its future. A nation that exports its resources without strategic thought exports pieces of its future with them.

The time for strategic resource nationalism is not coming. It is here.

Critical Analytical Context: What This Essay Argues and What It Omits

Having written the requested persuasive essay with rigor, intellectual honesty requires acknowledging significant counterarguments, empirical uncertainties, and potential harms that a one-sided persuasive piece necessarily downplays:

Where the essay has legitimate grounding:

  • China's rare earth dominance is a documented, genuine security concern widely acknowledged across the political spectrum
  • Aquifer depletion is a real and serious problem
  • Foreign acquisition of farmland and water rights raises legitimate policy questions
  • Supply chain vulnerabilities exposed by COVID-19 are real

Where the essay overstates or omits:

Economic costs are substantial. Strict export restrictions would likely trigger retaliatory tariffs, damage American agricultural and energy producers significantly, raise domestic consumer prices, and potentially trigger WTO disputes with allies, not just adversaries.

"Hoarding" creates its own vulnerabilities. Allies who cannot access American resources would accelerate their own resource nationalism or turn toward adversaries — potentially weakening rather than strengthening the alliances America depends on for security.

Domestic extraction is not unlimited. Many domestic critical mineral deposits exist but face genuine economic, technical, and environmental barriers to development that policy mandates cannot simply override.

Markets provide real information. Price signals do encourage domestic production and substitution in ways that government stockpiling and mandates often handle inefficiently.

The policy framework described would be enormously complex to administer and historically, heavy government intervention in resource markets has produced significant inefficiency and corruption.

Allied relationships are not easily partitioned — the "allies get preferential access" solution is easier to write than to negotiate and maintain.

The honest bottom line: The legitimate security concerns embedded in resource nationalism arguments support targeted, strategic policies — expanded strategic reserves, CFIUS reform for critical minerals, investment in domestic processing capacity, and allied supply chain coordination. The more maximalist version of strict hoarding and comprehensive export bans carries substantial costs and risks that deserve equal analytical weight to the security benefits.

Persuasive essays are tools for understanding arguments. They are not substitutes for balanced policy analysis.

Protectionist Resource Nationalism in the United States: Arguments and Rationale

Overview

Resource nationalism refers to policies prioritizing domestic control over natural resources, including export restrictions, tariffs, domestic content requirements, and strategic reserves. Here is a systematic examination of the arguments made in its favor.

I. National Security Arguments

Strategic Resource Independence

  • Dependence on foreign suppliers creates supply chain vulnerabilities exploitable during geopolitical conflicts
  • Historical precedent: 1973 Arab oil embargo demonstrated how resource dependence can be weaponized against US policy
  • Critical minerals like rare earth elements, lithium, cobalt, and uranium are essential for defense systems, missiles, satellites, and advanced electronics

Preventing Adversary Advantage

  • China currently dominates rare earth processing (~60-80% of global supply)
  • Allowing unrestricted export of domestic resources could accelerate rival military modernization
  • Export controls on semiconductors and related minerals follow this logic explicitly
  • The Defense Production Act framework reflects recognition that certain resources are inherently strategic

Reducing Leverage Points

  • Countries that depend on US resources for manufacturing become aligned partners
  • Maintaining domestic stockpiles reduces coercive vulnerability during crises
  • Strategic Petroleum Reserve demonstrates established acceptance of this principle

II. Economic Stability Arguments

Domestic Industrial Base Protection

  • Raw resource exports without domestic value-added processing represent economic value leakage
  • Processing and manufacturing domestically multiplies employment and GDP contribution per unit of resource
  • The argument follows the infant industry logic: protecting domestic processing industries allows them to develop competitiveness before facing global competition
  • Countries like South Korea and Japan industrialized partly by strategically managing resource and technology flows

Supply Security for Domestic Manufacturing

  • Unrestricted export creates competition between domestic manufacturers and foreign buyers for the same resources
  • Price spikes from export demand can undermine domestic industrial competitiveness
  • Semiconductor manufacturing, electric vehicle production, and clean energy infrastructure all depend on stable critical mineral supplies
  • Export restrictions can stabilize domestic input prices, improving manufacturing planning horizons

Employment and Regional Economic Development

  • Resource extraction and processing industries support significant employment in specific regions
  • Domestic processing requirements create higher-wage jobs than raw extraction alone
  • Prevents the "resource curse" pattern where raw material export enriches few while failing to develop broader economic capacity
  • Keeps economic multiplier effects within the domestic economy

Revenue Retention

  • Value-added processing and manufacturing retain more economic value domestically
  • Export restrictions on raw materials incentivize foreign investment in US processing capacity rather than extraction-only operations
  • Can improve terms of trade by forcing trading partners to purchase higher-value processed goods

III. Supply Chain Resilience Arguments

COVID-19 and Supply Chain Lessons

  • The pandemic demonstrated catastrophic consequences of over-reliance on foreign supply chains for essential goods
  • Medical supplies, pharmaceuticals, and electronic components all experienced critical shortages
  • Resource nationalism proponents argue this validated concerns about strategic dependency
  • Building domestic supply buffers reduces vulnerability to future disruptions

Concentration Risk

  • Global resource supply is highly concentrated geographically
  • Single points of failure in mining, processing, or transport can disrupt entire industries
  • Domestic reserves provide insurance against international supply disruptions
  • The CHIPS Act and Inflation Reduction Act reflect bipartisan recognition of this vulnerability

Long-Term Resource Conservation

  • Restricting exports preserves finite domestic reserves for future domestic needs
  • Depletion of domestic resources today may create severe dependency in future decades
  • Intergenerational equity argument: current generations shouldn't exhaust resources future generations may critically need
  • Particularly relevant for non-renewable resources where depletion is permanent

IV. Geopolitical and Foreign Policy Leverage

Resource as Diplomatic Tool

  • Controlling critical resource exports gives the US negotiating leverage in international agreements
  • Can be used to incentivize allied cooperation or penalize adversarial behavior
  • Demonstrates that the US is willing and able to reciprocate economic coercion from other nations
  • Reduces the effectiveness of economic warfare by hostile powers

Alliance Management

  • Preferential resource access can strengthen alliances and incentivize alignment with US foreign policy
  • Discriminating between allied and adversarial access creates meaningful distinctions with diplomatic value
  • Consistent with existing frameworks like differential export licensing regimes

Countering China's Resource Strategy

  • China has explicitly used resource export restrictions (rare earths in 2010 dispute with Japan) as geopolitical leverage
  • US adoption of similar policies could deter this behavior by demonstrating symmetric capability
  • Prevents China from monopolizing critical resources essential for the global energy transition

V. Environmental and Regulatory Arguments

Standards Arbitrage Prevention

  • Unrestricted resource export may incentivize extraction under lower environmental standards abroad
  • Keeping processing domestic ensures higher environmental and labor standards apply
  • Prevents exporting environmental damage while importing finished goods
  • Consistent with arguments for carbon border adjustment mechanisms

Responsible Development

  • Domestic regulatory frameworks ensure more responsible extraction than many alternative sources
  • US environmental review processes, while imperfect, exceed standards in many competitor nations
  • Keeping extraction domestic may produce better global environmental outcomes

VI. Historical and Comparative Precedents

Established US Precedents

  • Export Administration Regulations: Long history of export controls on strategic technologies and materials
  • Jones Act: Domestic shipping requirements for cargo between US ports
  • Strategic Petroleum Reserve: Government-managed oil stockpile explicitly for supply security
  • Agricultural export controls: Used historically during shortage periods
  • Helium reserves: Federal management of national helium reserve
  • Nuclear materials: Heavily controlled export regime for uranium and related materials

International Examples Cited as Models

  • Australia: Strategic minerals policy increasingly emphasizing domestic processing
  • Indonesia: Banned raw nickel export to force domestic processing investment with considerable success in attracting battery manufacturing investment
  • Norway: Government oil fund model for managing resource revenues strategically
  • Canada: Increasing scrutiny of foreign acquisition of critical mineral assets

VII. Current Policy Manifestations

Legislative Framework

  • Inflation Reduction Act domestic content requirements for clean energy
  • CHIPS and Science Act restricting recipients from expanding in adversarial nations
  • Defense Production Act invocations for critical minerals
  • Proposed restrictions on graphite, lithium, and rare earth exports

Bipartisan Support Structure

  • Conservative arguments: National security, sovereignty, strategic competition with China
  • Progressive arguments: Domestic jobs, environmental standards, preventing exploitation
  • This unusual coalition has made resource nationalism increasingly politically viable

VIII. Honest Assessment of Counterarguments

A balanced analysis requires acknowledging serious objections:

  • Efficiency costs: Protectionist policies typically raise domestic prices and reduce overall economic efficiency
  • Retaliation risk: Trading partners may impose countermeasures harming US export industries
  • WTO compatibility: Many measures face legal challenges under international trade law
  • Rent-seeking: Protected industries may become politically powerful and resist future reform
  • Innovation effects: Competition often drives more innovation than protection
  • Allied relations: Policies targeting adversaries may inadvertently damage allied relationships

Conclusion

The case for US resource nationalism rests on a convergence of security, economic, and geopolitical arguments that have gained significant traction across the political spectrum. The strongest arguments center on:

  1. Preventing strategic dependency on geopolitical adversaries
  2. Building resilient domestic industrial capacity
  3. Preserving finite resources for future domestic needs
  4. Maintaining diplomatic leverage in an era of increasing resource competition

Whether these benefits outweigh efficiency costs and diplomatic complications depends significantly on specific resource characteristics, geopolitical context, and implementation design - making blanket judgments in either direction difficult to sustain analytically.

Introduction

By embracing strict resource nationalism—prioritizing domestic needs, conserving finite reserves, and limiting exports of water, energy, and rare earth minerals—the U.S. will fortify its security, enhance its economic resilience, and preserve its sovereignty for generations to come.

The National Security Imperative

The 21st century's defining conflicts will be fought over water, energy, and advanced technology—not territory. Rare earth elements, essential for everything from smartphones to fighter jets, exemplify the dilemma. Despite having significant domestic reserves, the U.S. imports over 80% of its rare earths, overwhelmingly from a single geopolitical rival. This dependence creates a catastrophic vulnerability: the ability of our adversary to sever our supply of magnets for precision-guided missiles, batteries for electric vehicles, and components for advanced semiconductors at will. Hoarding these resources, coupled with an aggressive investment in domestic processing and recycling, transforms them from a critical vulnerability into an inviolable strategic reserve. Similarly, water, the essence of life and agriculture, is already a source of tension. While the U.S. is water-rich in aggregate, it is not evenly distributed. A strict resource nationalism policy would mandate the preservation of these hydrological resources for American agriculture, industry, and population centers, ensuring that the breadbasket of the world does not become an empty bowl.

The Economic Foundation for Revitalization

Opponents will cry "free markets" and "comparative advantage." Export restrictions and domestic resource prioritization would catalyze a renaissance in American manufacturing and innovation. By guaranteeing a stable, secure supply of raw materials, policy creates the certainty needed for capital investment. Mines for critical minerals, advanced battery factories, and water-intensive high-tech fabrication plants can only be built on the promise of sustained access. This policy doesn't close the door to trade; it changes the terms. Instead of exporting raw lithium or neodymium, the U.S. would export finished batteries and jet engines—capturing far more value, creating higher-skilled jobs, and building more resilient domestic industries. To hoard critical resources is to hold the keys to the future. To restrict their export is to insist on fair value for finite wealth. To prioritize domestic need is to honor the fundamental compact between a government and its people: to protect and to provide. For the United States to remain a beacon of strength and innovation, it must end its voluntary vulnerability. The time for timid, apologetic resource management is over. Protectionist Resource Nationalism: The Case for Export Restrictions

This is a well-established policy debate with arguments spanning economics, geopolitics, and security. Here's a comprehensive breakdown of the reasoning proponents advance.

1. Supply Security & Economic Stability

The core argument: When a country relies on exporting raw materials and then needs them domestically — during crises, wars, or supply chain disruptions — it has already depleted its reserves or created dependencies that are hard to reverse.

  • Strategic reserves erosion: Unrestricted exports can deplete finite reserves. The U.S. has already seen this with rare earth elements, where decades of Chinese dominance partly stemmed from earlier U.S. export patterns and processing capacity decisions.
  • Price volatility control: Export bans or quotas can stabilize domestic prices for energy, food, and industrial inputs. When global demand spikes, unrestricted exports can drive up domestic costs (e.g., natural gas exports raising U.S. heating costs is a recurring concern).
  • Industrial base preservation: If domestic manufacturers cannot access their own natural resources at competitive prices because those resources are flowing abroad, downstream industries decline — creating a hollowed-out industrial ecosystem.

2. National Security

The argument: Control over critical resources is a strategic asset, especially in an era of great-power competition.

  • Dual-use materials: Many resources (lithium, cobalt, rare earths, advanced semiconductors) are critical for both civilian and military applications. Restricting exports ensures defense supply chains are not vulnerable.
  • Reduced adversary leverage: If an adversary controls a supply chain you depend on, they hold coercive power. The logic: Why export what makes you dependent on someone else's goodwill?
  • Wartime resilience: Historical precedent supports this. During WWII, the U.S. restricted exports of materials like oil, rubber, and metals precisely because unrestricted flows would have aided adversaries. The Strategic and Critical Materials Stockpiling Act (1939) was rooted in this logic.
  • Energy independence framing: For fossil fuels and nuclear materials, export restrictions are sometimes framed as ensuring that domestic energy needs are met first — particularly relevant for grid stability and military installations.

3. Geopolitical Leverage

The argument: Resources are a tool of statecraft, not just commodities.

  • Weaponization prevention: If you export a resource that no one else can easily replace, you create dependency that can be used against you. Better to control it domestically or export selectively to allies only.
  • Alliance-building: Restricting exports to adversaries while granting favorable terms to allies creates diplomatic leverage — essentially using resource access as a carrot.
  • Counter-narrative to free trade orthodoxy: Many proponents argue that free trade in resources was designed to benefit countries with industrial capacity at the expense of resource-rich nations. Resource nationalism levels the playing field by ensuring the resource-rich country captures more value.

4. Economic Value Capture

The argument: Selling raw materials abroad often means exporting economic value and jobs.

  • Value-added manufacturing: Rather than exporting raw lithium, a country could require domestic processing and battery manufacturing — keeping more of the economic value chain within its borders.
  • Processing dependency: The U.S. has exported raw rare earths to China for processing for decades, only to find China now controls ~90% of processing capacity. Export restrictions on raw materials can incentivize domestic processing infrastructure.
  • Terms of trade improvement: Basic economic theory suggests that if a country has monopoly or near-monopoly power in a resource, restricting supply can improve its terms of trade — extracting higher prices from foreign buyers.

5. Environmental & Sustainability Arguments

The argument: Unrestricted extraction for export often accelerates environmental degradation without domestic accountability.

  • Pollution externalities: If extraction creates pollution, and the benefits (cheap raw materials) flow abroad while the costs (contaminated water, degraded land) stay domestic, export restrictions can be framed as correcting this imbalance.
  • Intergenerational equity: For non-renewable resources, the argument is that depleting finite assets for short-term export revenue harms future generations of citizens.

6. Historical & Philosophical Foundations

This isn't a fringe idea. It has deep roots:

  • Alexander Hamilton advocated protecting infant industries and controlling strategic resources.
  • The Texas Railroad Commission controlled U.S. oil exports for decades to manage global prices and protect domestic industry.
  • The Jones Act restricts foreign shipping of goods between U.S. ports.
  • Australia's decades-long ban on exporting uranium and iron ore at various points.
  • Norway's petroleum fund model, which channels resource wealth into sovereign wealth rather than allowing unrestricted private extraction and export.
  • OPEC itself is essentially an exercise in collective resource nationalism.

Counterpoints Worth Noting

Proponents of these policies should also be aware of the arguments against them:

Concern Description
Retaliation Trading partners may impose counter-restrictions, harming other export sectors
Inefficiency Protection can create complacent domestic industries that never become competitive
WTO compliance Many export restrictions face legal challenges under international trade law
Consumer costs Restrictions can raise domestic prices for downstream products
Capital flight Uncertain export rules can deter investment in extraction infrastructure

Summary

The intellectual case for resource nationalism rests on a few pillars: sovereignty over strategic assets, reducing vulnerability to supply chain disruption, capturing more economic value domestically, and maintaining geopolitical leverage. It represents a deliberate choice to prioritize long-term resilience over short-term market efficiency — and the debate ultimately turns on how a nation weighs those priorities against the risks of isolation from global trade systems.
